My origin story starts in a weird place: video games.

How games sparked my interest

I played UFC 2009 Undisputed, EA Sports MMA, and Tekken 3. They made me curious about combat sports.

Games sparked questions. Real skills took practice with a coach.

After a loss, I wanted to know what went wrong. After a win, I wanted to test the next idea. I bring that habit to coaching.

What I saw in PRIDE

I watched PRIDE fights and saw styles meet. A skilled striker could still struggle in a hold. That made me want to learn grappling.

PRIDE gave me more questions about the ground game. PRIDE Fighting Championships

Strikes and holds change the space in a fight. Grappling can decide who gets to move.

I wanted to learn more about grappling.

What I learned from ADCC

ADCC is a major no-gi grappling contest. Watching it led me to study the BJJ roots of some athletes.

ADCC gave me a reason to study basic skills. ADCC Submission Fighting World Championship

Many athletes train in more than one setting. Gi practice can teach grips, stance, and escapes. These skills need work to fit a no-gi round. Learn the class words

My lesson: build a base you can use under pressure.

What I teach in class

1) Build basic skills

  • Posture you can keep when tired.
  • Frames that help you keep space.
  • Escapes against a partner’s pressure.
  • Top holds against active partners.

2) Learn how strikes change the task

  • Where to keep your head for protection.
  • How strikes change guard choices.
  • How to hold close and improve your spot.
  • How to stand when you need to leave the ground.

3) Use the gi as a learning tool

Gi drills can make some skills easier to study. Learn the class words

  • Grips and ways to break them.
  • A steady stance.
  • Time to feel and fix a step.

Then we adapt the grips to no-gi. We work on arm hooks, head position, and body holds. We add safe get-ups and resets.

Can you do MMA if you train in the gi?

Gi skills can be part of that path. You still need MMA-specific training.

MMA also needs strikes, wrestling, and cage skills. Gi practice gives you some tools. Each tool needs practice in the right setting. Learn how strikes change a hold or escape.

The aim is to adapt basic skills with care.

What to ask a coach

  • Can they explain why a move works?
  • Do they teach escapes as well as holds?
  • Do they teach safe get-ups?
  • Do they explain how sport rules differ?
  • Do they set limits for partner care?

Build a clear base

Start with a few core skills. Ask your coach how to practice them.

  1. How to breathe under pressure.
  2. How to frame and recover guard.
  3. How to escape bad positions.
  4. How to hold top position.
  5. How to stand up safely.

FAQ: Sensei MMA BJJ

What does "sensei" mean in MMA and BJJ?

Sensei means teacher. A coach should guide your learning and care for students. Ask how they teach safe partner work.

Is BJJ enough for MMA?

MMA uses BJJ, strikes, wrestling, and cage skills. BJJ helps you hold, escape, and choose when to get up. MMA needs practice across those skills.

Should I train gi or no-gi for MMA?

Both can help in different ways. Gi teaches grips and control. No-gi uses other holds and a different pace. Ask your coach what fits your goal. See paid plans
